summary: A small Alpine country between Switzerland and Austria, one of the few doubly landlocked countries in the world. The princely family holds considerable real power, and the country is known for its financial sector and precision industry.

ranking.name: Catholicism
ranking.description: Christianity reached the Rhine Valley in the 4th–5th centuries. During the 16th-century Reformation the local rulers maintained the Catholic faith, so the principality, like neighboring Vorarlberg in Austria and the Catholic regions of Switzerland, remained Catholic. The 1921 constitution made Catholicism the state religion, and the Archdiocese of Vaduz was established in 1997. It is still the largest religion in the country, although the government is now discussing the separation of church and state.

ranking.name: Protestantism
ranking.description: Liechtenstein itself did not experience the Reformation. Protestants are mainly immigrants from Switzerland and Germany who arrived in the 19th–20th centuries and their descendants, mostly belonging to evangelical (Lutheran and Reformed) churches, which have their own churches in places such as Vaduz.

ranking.name: No religion
ranking.description: After World War II Liechtenstein changed from an agricultural country into an industrial and financial center. With economic prosperity and rising levels of education, a trend toward secularization appeared as in other European countries, and the number of people who have left the church or belong to no religion has gradually increased, mainly among the younger generation.

ranking.name: Islam
ranking.description: During the period of rapid economic growth in the 1960s–70s, Liechtenstein recruited foreign workers from Turkey and the former Yugoslavia, who brought Islam with them. Today Muslims are mainly immigrants from Turkey, Bosnia and Kosovo and their descendants.

religion.background: The Rhine Valley, where Liechtenstein lies, belonged to the Roman province of Raetia in Roman times. Christianity arrived in the 4th–5th centuries, and the area long belonged to the Diocese of Chur in Switzerland. During the 16th-century Reformation the local rulers remained Catholic, so Liechtenstein, like Austria and the Catholic cantons of Switzerland, kept the Catholic faith. In 1719 the House of Liechtenstein merged two territories into a principality of the Holy Roman Empire, and it became independent in 1806. The constitution made Catholicism the state religion, and in 1997 the Pope established the Archdiocese of Vaduz, separating it from the Diocese of Chur. In recent years immigration and secularization have made the religious composition increasingly diverse.

ranking.name: German (Alemannic dialect)
ranking.description: The inhabitants of Liechtenstein already spoke the Alemannic dialect of German in the Middle Ages, which is very close to Swiss German and to the dialect of Vorarlberg in Austria. The 1921 constitution made German the official language; schools, administration and the media use Standard German, while everyday life is conducted mainly in the dialect.

ranking.name: Italian
ranking.description: Italian speakers are mainly migrant workers who came from Italy after World War II and their descendants, who took part in Liechtenstein's industrial development and infrastructure projects in the 1950s–60s.

ranking.name: Portuguese
ranking.description: Most Portuguese speakers are workers who have immigrated from Portugal in recent decades, mainly employed in construction and services, in line with the trend of Switzerland and Liechtenstein bringing in large numbers of Portuguese workers at the time.

ranking.name: Turkish
ranking.description: Turkish speakers mainly come from the Turkish foreign workers recruited during the economic take-off of the 1960s–70s and their families, and some have acquired Liechtenstein citizenship.

language.history: In Roman times the Rhine Valley used Latin, and later developed Raeto-Romance, which is close to today's Romansh of Switzerland. In the 5th–6th centuries the Germanic Alemanni moved in, and after several hundred years of language shift, by the late Middle Ages the local inhabitants had come to speak Alemannic German dialects, although many place names still preserve Romance origins. The 1921 constitution made German the official language; schools and the government use Standard German, while the Alemannic dialect is used in daily life.

ranking.name: Cheese Knöpfle
ranking.description: Small dumplings made from flour, eggs and water, mixed with plenty of local cheese (such as Sauerkäse), topped with fried onions and often served with applesauce.
ranking.history: Käsknöpfle is Liechtenstein's most representative home-style dish, rooted in the life of Alpine dairy farmers: mountain dwellers made long-keeping cheese from milk and combined it with cheap flour to make a filling staple. The dish resembles the cheese spaetzle (Käsespätzle) of neighboring Vorarlberg in Austria and southern Germany, reflecting the food culture that Liechtenstein shares with the surrounding Alemannic-speaking regions.

ranking.name: Ribel (crumbled corn fry)
ranking.description: Coarse cornmeal cooked with milk or water into a paste, then stir-fried in a pan into crumbs and eaten with applesauce, coffee or cheese. It is crisp, with a faint sweetness of corn.
ranking.history: Corn reached Europe from the Americas in the 16th–17th centuries. The mild climate of the Rhine Valley suited its cultivation, and a white corn variety (Rheintaler Ribel) became the staple food of local farmers. Ribel was once the breakfast and dinner of the poor and was gradually replaced by other foods in the 20th century, but in recent years it has regained appreciation through the Slow Food movement, and the white Rhine Valley corn has also been certified by Switzerland as a protected designation of origin product.

ranking.name: Swiss rösti
ranking.description: Grated potatoes fried in a pan with butter or oil into a large golden cake, crisp outside and soft inside. It can be a side dish to a main course, or have cheese, bacon or a fried egg added.
ranking.history: Rösti was originally the breakfast of farmers in the Swiss canton of Bern. After the 18th century potatoes became common in the Alpine region and replaced the more expensive grains. Liechtenstein and Switzerland concluded a customs union in 1923 and use the Swiss franc, and the food cultures of the two countries are very close, so rösti has become a common side dish on Liechtenstein tables.

ranking.name: Cheese fondue
ranking.description: Cheese and white wine are heated and melted in a ceramic pot, and pieces of bread are dipped in the melted cheese with long forks. It has a rich flavor with the aroma of white wine and cheese, and is a winter gathering dish.
ranking.history: Fondue is generally thought to have originated in the Swiss Alps, and a cookbook from Zurich in 1699 already records cheese cooked with wine. In winter, mountain farmers made it with stored cheese and hard bread, making effective use of leftover food. In the 1930s the Swiss Cheese Union promoted fondue as a national dish, and Liechtenstein was also influenced by this, often eating cheese fondue at winter and festive gatherings.

ranking.name: Fried sausage
ranking.description: A smoked sausage made from pork and beef, sliced and pan-fried or grilled, often served with potato salad or onion sauce. It tastes salty and savory with a smoky aroma.
ranking.history: Schüblig is a sausage common in the St. Gallen area of eastern Switzerland and in Liechtenstein, and belongs to the shared meat-product tradition of the Alemannic-speaking region. In the Alpine region, processed pork products were an important way for farm households to preserve meat over winter, made after pigs were slaughtered each autumn and winter. Today it often appears at festival markets, sporting events and family barbecues.
